targets.authors: Chetty, Raj, John N. Friedman and Jonah E. Rockoff.
targets.title: Measuring the Impacts of Teachers I: Evaluating Bias in Teacher Value-Added Estimates.
targets.evidence_quote: In this paper, we replicated the CFR analysis using data from the Los Angeles Unified School District and similarly found that teacher value-added estimates were valid predictors of student achievement.
targets.outcome_quote: Second, the heterogeneity in teacher effects was considerably larger in Los Angeles than in New York City. The consequences for math or English achievement of being assigned a top rather than a bottom quartile teacher in Los Angeles were nearly twice as large as in New York. Third, unlike CFR, we found statistically significant differences in average effectiveness of the teachers by student race/ethnicity and by prior achievement scores.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Forecast validity confirms CFR; authors explicitly contrast significant sorting differences with CFR. Confirmation of one effect does not override contrasts on other retested findings.

targets.title: Revisiting the Impacts of Teachers.
targets.evidence_quote: In addition to replicating the CFR and Rothstein analyses, we extended their work in three ways.
targets.outcome_quote: In a recent paper, Rothstein (2014) reports a statistically significant relationship between change in teacher value-added and changes in baseline achievement as prima facie evidence of bias in the CFR method. We find similar results, but offer a different interpretation. We find that the predicted change has a coefficient of .268 when lagged scores are the dependent variable. However, rather than invalidating the CFR methodology, the lagged score test merely demonstrates the hazards of using the same data to estimate the dependent and 19 independent variables.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Statistical placebo relationship is replicated but shown to be mechanically confounded, a central methodological critique.

targets.title: Match Quality, Worker Productivity, and Worker Mobility: Direct Evidence From Teachers.
targets.evidence_quote: Using data from North Carolina, Jackson (forthcoming) estimates that teacher-school match effects account for roughly one-third of the variance in teacher effects. To test the possibility that teacher effects vary by context, we first divide the data available for each teacher’s value-added into value-added estimates using observations only from the same school and those from all available schools.
targets.outcome_quote: Consistent with Jackson’s findings regarding teacher-school matches, the point estimate on value-added estimate of the same school, 1.054, is larger than the coefficient on the difference between that from all schools and similar schools, .817. However, we could not reject the hypothesis that both coefficients were equal to one (p value=.163).
targets.outcome_reasoning: Authors describe the direction as consistent with Jackson. Equality cannot be rejected; this tentative outcome follows their comparison, not statistical significance.

reasoning: Different district sample retests CFR, Rothstein placebo findings, and Jackson school-context specificity. Other validation studies are background. Jackson is cited as forthcoming.
